deep_research_task.objective: Study the process-orchestration failure modes of a cross-vendor, CLI-driven multi-agent coding harness ("Foreman") and identify open-source frameworks, libraries, or proven patterns that could replace or harden its home-grown orchestration layer. Produce an evidence-based recommendation: adopt X / adapt Y / keep building in-house, with migration cost estimates.

system_under_study.description: Foreman is an architect/worker orchestration harness for AI coding agents. A high-judgment "architect" model decomposes work into five-part specs and routes them to cheaper worker lanes, each lane a headless CLI subprocess of a DIFFERENT vendor (xAI `grok` CLI for implementation, OpenAI `codex` CLI for audit at high reasoning effort, Anthropic Claude subagents as wrappers/advisors). Every lane runs in an isolated git worktree and must write a report file before exit. A cross-vendor invariant (auditor vendor != implementer vendor) gates merges. Being built now: an append-only per-run event log (events.jsonl) as source of truth, git-plumbing worktree checkpoints (refs/checkpoints/*), a NATS JetStream one-way transport for watchers, a stall watchdog (RUNNING->STALLED->DEAD state machine), and resume-from-checkpoint.
system_under_study.environment: Windows 11 host; lanes run under Git Bash (MSYS2) with WSL2 available but unstable under load; bash + git plumbing + jq + bats-core; NATS JetStream available; no Docker requirement in the default ("soft") mode; no flock (mkdir mutexes); CRLF hazards everywhere.

observed_failures.failure: A grok CLI subprocess outlived its wrapper's 600s timeout by 45+ minutes (timeout fired without killing the process GROUP), leaving the lane blocked on a dead-end pipe, 50+ orphaned bash processes host-wide, and the lane's completed work stranded. Killing the one stale PID released 18 blocked shells instantly.

Wrapper agents background their CLI call and end their turn "to wait", producing ambiguous lane state: agent reports finished, no report file written, subprocess still writing to the worktree. Required manual resume, twice on the same lane.

Four concurrently dispatched grok lanes ran effectively single-file (exactly one grok process alive; all four worktrees write-quiet for the first 10 minutes) — suspected account-level queuing or a config/session lock in the vendor CLI. Worktree parallelism did not translate into wall-clock parallelism.

File-mtime stall watchdogs false-alarm on read/reason-heavy phases (auditors are quiet by design for 20+ min), on completed lanes, and on verification phases (test suites write nothing to the worktree). No QUEUED vs RUNNING vs VERIFYING distinction exists. Conversely a truly hung lane (F1) looked identical to a busy one for ~45 minutes.

failure.name: mid-response API deaths lose lane context

observed_failures.failure: A wrapper died to a transient server error seconds into its round with zero progress signal; a lane dying deep into an implementation would lose everything since dispatch (motivates checkpoints + resume).

failure.name: drifted parallel history from remote lane

observed_failures.failure: A remote (cloud) agent lane produced a 55-commit branch sharing NO git ancestor with main (rebuilt history), while main independently evolved past the architecture the branch splices into — no mechanical merge path; file-by-file re-port now required.

research_questions.q: Which open-source orchestration/durable-execution frameworks natively solve F1/F2/F5 — i.e., PID/process-group-owned child lifecycles, hard timeout-with-group-kill, heartbeats, checkpoint/replay, and resume-after-crash — and can wrap arbitrary subprocesses (vendor CLIs we do not control)? Evaluate at minimum: Temporal (+ its lighter alternatives: LittleHorse, Inngest, Hatchet, Windmill, restate.dev), Prefect, Dagster, Airflow (only if warranted), Ray (core + workflows), Celery/RQ-class queues, and supervision-only options (supervisord, systemd user services, s6/runit, pueue, nq). For each: Windows/Git-Bash viability WITHOUT Docker, bash-first ergonomics, footprint, and whether durable state survives host restart.

Which AI-agent-specific orchestration frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen/AG2, CrewAI, OpenAI Swarm successors, claude-flow, OpenHands, SWE-agent/ mini-SWE-agent harnesses, Aider scripting mode, plandex, goose, etc.) have production-grade answers for multi-CLI-vendor lanes — not just LLM-API orchestration? Specifically: subprocess lifecycle management, per-lane sandboxes/worktrees, crash resume, and observable lane state. Distinguish "orchestrates API calls" from "orchestrates OS processes" — we need the latter.

Liveness/health patterns for agent lanes (F4): what do mature CI systems (GitHub Actions runners, GitLab runners, Buildkite agents, BuildBarn/ Bazel remote execution workers) use to distinguish QUEUED / RUNNING / VERIFYING / HUNG — heartbeat protocols, output-stream activity vs file activity, exec probes? Which of these transfer to a bash event-log architecture? Cite concrete heartbeat interval / grace-period defaults they ship with.

Vendor CLI concurrency (F3): documented concurrency semantics/limits of the xAI grok CLI, OpenAI codex CLI, and Claude Code headless mode as of 2026-07 — per-account session locks, parallel invocation support, isolated-config-dir workarounds (e.g. per-lane GROK_CONFIG_DIR / CODEX_HOME), and any official guidance on running N instances on one machine. Include rate-limit vs local-lock disambiguation techniques.

For F6: what conventions/tooling do multi-agent or multi-repo projects use to guarantee remote lanes stay mergeable — branch-freshness checks, merge-base CI gates, bot-driven rebase cadence (Renovate/dependabot-style for branches), stacked-diff tools (Graphite, git-branchless, jj/Jujutsu)? Would Jujutsu's operation-log/undo model materially help a checkpoint-heavy agent workflow on Windows?

Is there prior art for an EVENT LOG + object-store checkpoint design for agent harnesses specifically (event-sourced agent runs, replayable transcripts)? Compare our events.jsonl + refs/checkpoints design against what LangGraph checkpointers, Temporal histories, and OpenHands trajectories persist; identify anything we should copy (schemas, compaction, cursor semantics) before our design ossifies.

evaluation_criteria.criterion: Solves F1/F2 outright (process-group ownership, group-kill on timeout, no orphan possible by construction)
Windows 11 + Git Bash native (no Docker/WSL dependency; WSL2 on this host crash-reboots under load)
Wraps arbitrary vendor CLIs we do not control; bash-first integration; no SDK lock-in for lane code
Durable state + resume (survives wrapper death, host restart); event-log compatible
Observability: per-lane state machine visible without parsing logs; queue-aware (QUEUED != STALLED)
Footprint/complexity: runnable by one developer; no always-on cluster; degrades gracefully offline
License (permissive preferred) + project health (commits/releases in last 6 months, bus factor)

method_requirements.requirement: Every factual claim carries a source URL and an accessed date; docs change fast — prefer 2025-2026 sources; mark single-source claims UNVERIFIED.
Test claims against the Windows/Git-Bash constraint explicitly — a framework that is Linux-only in practice must say so in the first line of its assessment, not the last.
Separate "framework solves it" from "framework provides primitives you must assemble" — estimate assembly effort in days for the latter.

Include at least one option in the final matrix that is NOT a framework adoption: hardening the existing bash harness with targeted primitives (Windows Job Objects via a small helper, `timeout --kill-after`, pueue as a lane queue, etc.).
No vendor marketing language; where benchmarks are quoted, note methodology.

output_format.section: Executive summary (max 1 page): the single recommended path and the two runners-up, with the decisive reasons.
Failure-mode coverage matrix: rows F1-F6, columns = evaluated candidates, cells = solves / partial (what remains) / no.
Per-candidate assessments (the 5-8 serious ones only): what it is, process-lifecycle model, Windows reality, integration sketch with our lane-run.sh/event-log design, effort estimate, license/health.
Q3 liveness patterns: concrete state-machine + heartbeat design recommendation with the CI-industry defaults cited.
Q4 vendor CLI concurrency findings with workarounds ranked by risk.
Q5/Q6 findings: merge-freshness gate design + event-log schema deltas worth adopting.
Recommended 30/60/90-day adoption plan for the winning option, sized for one architect + cheap worker lanes.
Full source list with accessed dates.
